chunks: And from him, from Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from Ibn Abi Umayr, from Ziyad al-Qandi, from Abdullah ibn Sinan, from Abu al-Hasan (peace be upon him), who said:
I said to him, 'Does the suckling (radha') prohibit marriage in the case of one, two, or three sucklings?' He said, 'No, except that which makes the bone firm and the flesh grow.'.

If it is said, 'There is no mention of ten sucklings in any of these narrations, yet you have given the legal opinion that ten sucklings prohibit marriage,' it is said to him, 'They have explained in other narrations that that which makes the flesh grow and the bone firm firm is ten sucklings, so that sufficed for mentioning it here.'
Four [narrators]: Muhammad ibn Ya'qub narrated from a number of our companions, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from Ali ibn al-Hakam, from Mu'awiya ibn Wahb, from Ubayd ibn Zur'arah, who said:

I said to Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), 'We are a large family, and sometimes joy and sorrow gather men and women together in it. Sometimes the woman feels shy to uncover her head in front of the man with whom she has the relationship of suckling, and sometimes the man feels shy to look at that. So what is it from suckling that prohibits marriage?'

He said, 'That which makes the flesh and blood grow.' I said, 'So what is it that makes the flesh and blood grow?' He said, 'It was said: ten sucklings.' I said, 'So does marriage become prohibited by ten sucklings?' He said, 'Leave that.'.
And he said, 'That which prohibits marriage due to lineage (blood relation) is the same that prohibits it due to suckling.'
ai.seo_question: How many sucklings are required to prohibit marriage in Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: This narration from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam* highlights the jurisprudential tension between the qualitative criterion ('making flesh grow and bone firm') and the quantitative consensus of ten sucklings (*al-'ashr rad'aat*) in Shia fiqh. The Imam’s statement that 'what is prohibited by lineage is prohibited by suckling' establishes the theological basis for *mahramiyyah*, linking the physical act of nursing to the permanent kinship ties derived from blood, a principle deeply rooted in the Quranic verse 33:5.
